reviewStatus: Original educational pilot. Sources are provided for each concept; this is not official AAMC content.

concepts.title: Competitive enzyme inhibition
concepts.lesson: Reversible competitive inhibitors compete with substrate for the active site. At a given substrate concentration, the reaction slows. Enough substrate can outcompete the inhibitor, so Vmax stays the same, while the apparent Km increases: more substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax.
concepts.distinction: A slower reaction at one substrate concentration does not establish a lower Vmax. Look at the high-substrate plateau.

diagnostic.stem: A reversible inhibitor competes only with substrate for the active site. What should happen at very high substrate concentration?
options: The rate approaches the original Vmax
Vmax must fall to half its original value
The reaction equilibrium shifts toward substrate
diagnostic.explanation: Excess substrate can outcompete a reversible competitive inhibitor. The maximum catalytic rate is preserved.

checks.stem: An enzyme reaches 80 units/min without inhibitor. With compound X, twice as much substrate is needed to reach 40 units/min, but the high-substrate plateau remains 80. Which interpretation fits?
checks.explanation: Half-maximal rate is still 40. Needing more substrate there means a higher apparent Km; the plateau establishes an unchanged Vmax.

checks.stem: A reversible inhibitor slows an enzyme at low substrate concentration. A researcher adds much more substrate and fully restores the original maximal rate. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Removal of half of the enzyme molecules
checks.explanation: Full recovery with excess substrate supports competitive inhibition, rather than loss of functional enzyme or pure noncompetitive inhibition.

checks.stem: Two rate-versus-substrate curves reach the same plateau. Curve B is shifted right: its half-maximum occurs at 12 mM rather than 4 mM. What changed?
checks.explanation: The half-maximum concentration changed from 4 to 12 mM. The common plateau means Vmax is unchanged.

concepts.title: Buffers after adding strong acid
concepts.lesson: A buffer contains a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A−. Added strong acid first consumes A− and forms HA. Update those amounts before using pH = pKa + log10([A−]/[HA]). Equal amounts give pH = pKa. More conjugate base raises pH; more weak acid lowers it. This shortcut assumes both components remain in appreciable amounts.
concepts.distinction: Do the acid–base reaction first. The original ratio no longer applies after adding strong acid.

diagnostic.stem: A buffer initially has equal amounts of HA and A−. A small amount of strong acid is added. What happens first?
options: HA is consumed and A− forms
A− is consumed and HA forms
Both amounts stay exactly the same
The weak acid becomes a strong acid
diagnostic.explanation: The conjugate base accepts the added H+. The base/acid ratio falls.

checks.stem: A buffer contains 0.30 mol HA and 0.30 mol A−. Adding 0.10 mol HCl causes negligible volume change. Which ratio belongs in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation?
checks.explanation: HCl consumes 0.10 mol A−, leaving 0.20, and forms 0.10 mol HA, giving 0.40.

checks.stem: A buffer has pKa 6.0 and a conjugate-base/weak-acid ratio of 10. What is its approximate pH?
A buffer contains 0.40 mol HA and 0.20 mol A−. After adding 0.10 mol NaOH, what is the approximate pH relative to pKa?
options: Impossible because all HA is consumed
checks.explanation: OH− consumes 0.10 mol HA and creates 0.10 mol A−. Both amounts become 0.30 mol, so the ratio is 1.

concepts.title: Equilibrium versus reaction speed
concepts.lesson: Equilibrium describes composition when forward and reverse rates match. A catalyst speeds both directions and does not change the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature. Compressing a gas mixture favors the side with fewer gas molecules, when the sides have different gas stoichiometries. For an exothermic forward reaction, heating favors the reverse direction.
concepts.distinction: A faster approach to equilibrium does not necessarily produce more product at equilibrium.

diagnostic.stem: A catalyst is added to a reaction at equilibrium at fixed temperature. What changes?
options: Both directions become faster; equilibrium composition stays the same
Only the forward direction becomes faster
diagnostic.explanation: A catalyst lowers kinetic barriers in both directions without changing the equilibrium constant.

checks.stem: For 2X(g) ⇌ Y(g), the vessel volume is halved at constant temperature. Which shift restores equilibrium?
options: No shift because both species are gases
The direction depends only on catalyst concentration
checks.explanation: Compression favors fewer gas molecules: one Y rather than two X.

checks.stem: For A(g) ⇌ 2B(g), expansion occurs at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
options: The mixture shifts toward B; K stays constant
The mixture shifts toward B; K increases
A catalyst is required for any shift
The mixture shifts toward A; K stays constant
checks.explanation: Expansion favors the side with more gas molecules. At fixed temperature, K does not change.

checks.stem: The forward reaction releases heat. What does increasing temperature do to its equilibrium composition?
options: Has no effect on any equilibrium
Acts exactly like adding a catalyst
Always favors products because reactions run faster
checks.explanation: Treat heat as a product of an exothermic forward reaction. Adding heat favors the reverse direction.

concepts.title: Series versus parallel resistors
concepts.lesson: In series, every resistor carries the same current and resistances add. In parallel, every branch has the same voltage, currents add, and reciprocal resistances add. With an ideal fixed-voltage battery, adding a parallel branch lowers equivalent resistance and increases total current. Check that parallel resistance is smaller than the smallest branch resistance.
concepts.distinction: Identify the connections before using V = IR. Branch current and total battery current are different quantities.
diagram: Find equivalent R → use I = V/R

diagnostic.stem: Two resistors connect across the same two battery terminals. Which quantity must be equal for both resistors?
diagnostic.explanation: Parallel branches share the same two electrical nodes, so they have the same voltage.

checks.stem: Two 12 Ω resistors are connected in parallel across an ideal 6 V battery. What current does the battery supply?
checks.explanation: Two equal parallel resistors give 6 Ω. Total current is 6 V / 6 Ω = 1 A; each branch carries 0.5 A.

checks.stem: A 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor are in series across an ideal 12 V battery. What current flows through the 4 Ω resistor?
checks.explanation: Series resistance is 6 Ω. The same 12/6 = 2 A flows through both resistors.

checks.stem: A second identical resistor is added in parallel to a resistor on an ideal fixed-voltage battery. What happens to total battery current?
checks.explanation: The equivalent resistance halves, so total current doubles at fixed voltage.

concepts.title: DNA synthesis and proofreading
concepts.lesson: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a growing strand’s 3′ end, so synthesis proceeds 5′ to 3′. The template is read in the opposite direction. Proofreading removes a mismatched terminal nucleotide using 3′-to-5′ exonuclease activity. Removing proofreading increases errors without reversing the direction of synthesis.
concepts.distinction: The direction of error removal is not the direction in which the new strand grows.

diagnostic.stem: A DNA strand is growing during replication. Where does the polymerase add the next nucleotide?
options: The middle of a completed strand
diagnostic.explanation: Addition requires the growing strand’s free 3′ hydroxyl, producing 5′-to-3′ synthesis.

checks.stem: A polymerase retains nucleotide addition but loses proofreading. Which change is most likely?
options: RNA is synthesized instead of DNA
More mismatches remain in newly synthesized DNA
checks.explanation: Proofreading and polymerization are distinct activities. Losing correction increases errors without changing growth direction.

checks.stem: A template segment is written 3′-TACG-5′. Which new DNA strand is complementary and antiparallel?
checks.explanation: Base pairing gives A–T and G–C; the new DNA runs antiparallel to the template and contains T, not U.

checks.stem: A replicating polymerase has just inserted a mismatched base. Which activity can remove it from the growing terminus?
checks.explanation: Proofreading removes the incorrect nucleotide from the 3′ end before synthesis continues.

concepts.title: Family evidence and recessive inheritance
concepts.lesson: For a fully penetrant autosomal recessive condition, an affected child has genotype aa. If both biological parents are unaffected, assume the simple Mendelian model: each parent is Aa. Each pregnancy has a 1/4 chance of aa. Among unaffected children of Aa × Aa, the possible genotypes are AA, Aa, Aa, so the carrier probability is 2/3.
concepts.distinction: Use the family evidence when it is given. A population allele frequency does not replace known parental genotypes.

diagnostic.stem: Under a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model, two unaffected parents have an affected child. What are the parents’ genotypes?
diagnostic.explanation: The affected child received a recessive allele from each parent. Unaffected parents must therefore both be carriers.

checks.stem: Two carriers of a fully penetrant autosomal recessive condition have one affected child. What is the probability their next child is affected?
checks.explanation: Each pregnancy is an independent Aa × Aa cross. Prior outcomes do not change its 1/4 risk.

checks.stem: An unaffected child has two Aa parents. Under a fully penetrant recessive model, what is the probability the child is a carrier?
checks.explanation: Condition on being unaffected: exclude aa. Two of the remaining three equally weighted outcomes are Aa.

checks.stem: An Aa individual and an AA individual have a child. Under the simple fully penetrant recessive model, what is the chance of an affected child?
checks.explanation: The AA parent always contributes A, so the child can be AA or Aa, but not aa.

concepts.title: Classical conditioning: stimulus or response
concepts.lesson: An unconditioned stimulus elicits a response without the relevant training. A previously neutral cue becomes a conditioned stimulus after association with that event. The learned reaction to that cue is the conditioned response. Separate the event from the reaction, and ask whether its effect depended on learning.
concepts.distinction: The conditioned stimulus is the cue. The conditioned response is what the organism does or feels in response to it.

diagnostic.stem: After a tone is repeatedly paired with food, a dog salivates to the tone alone. What is the tone now?
diagnostic.explanation: The tone is a learned predictive cue. Salivation to it is the conditioned response.

checks.stem: A previously neutral clinic odor is repeatedly paired with a nausea-inducing procedure. Later, the odor alone elicits nausea. What is the nausea elicited by the odor?
checks.explanation: The nausea is a response. Because this reaction to the odor was learned, it is conditioned.

checks.stem: Before training, an air puff automatically elicits a blink. A light is then paired with the puff. What role does the air puff have?
checks.explanation: The air puff elicits blinking without the pairing history. It is the unconditioned stimulus.

checks.stem: After a bell is paired with food, a dog salivates to the bell. Which observation identifies a conditioned response?
options: The sound of the bell itself
The original salivation to food before pairing
Salivation when only the bell sounds
checks.explanation: Salivation to the learned cue is the conditioned response; the bell is the stimulus.

concepts.title: Reinforcement schedules
concepts.lesson: Ratio schedules depend on the number of responses. Interval schedules reward the first response after time has passed. Fixed schedules use a predictable requirement; variable schedules change it unpredictably. A variable-ratio schedule rewards an unpredictable response count. An interval schedule is not simply a reward delivered automatically on a clock.
concepts.distinction: First decide count versus time. Then decide predictable versus unpredictable.

diagnostic.stem: A reward follows every fifth button press. Which schedule is this?
diagnostic.explanation: The requirement is a response count, and it is predictable: five presses.

checks.stem: A researcher rewards the first lever press after an unpredictable waiting period. Which schedule is this?
checks.explanation: Eligibility depends on variable elapsed time, followed by a response, rather than a variable number of presses.

checks.stem: A reward occurs after 2, then 9, then 4 responses, with the required count unpredictable. Which schedule is this?
checks.explanation: The changing requirement counts responses, making this variable ratio.

checks.stem: The first response after each 60-second waiting period earns a reward. Which schedule is this?
checks.explanation: A predictable amount of elapsed time makes reinforcement available for the next response.

concepts.title: Reinforcement versus punishment
concepts.lesson: Reinforcement increases a behavior; punishment decreases it. Positive means adding a consequence, and negative means removing one. Classify by the observed change in behavior, not whether the consequence sounds pleasant. Removing an unpleasant sound and making a behavior more frequent is negative reinforcement.
concepts.distinction: Negative does not mean punishment. Use two decisions: added or removed, then behavior up or down.

diagnostic.stem: Buckling a seat belt stops a loud chime, and the driver begins buckling sooner. Which process strengthens buckling?
diagnostic.explanation: An unpleasant sound is removed and buckling increases: negative reinforcement.

checks.stem: A student loses game access after repeatedly interrupting. Interruptions become less frequent. What is this?
checks.explanation: Something is removed and the target behavior decreases: negative punishment.

checks.stem: A rat presses a lever, receives food, and subsequently presses more often. What process is operating?
checks.explanation: Food is added and lever pressing increases: positive reinforcement.

checks.stem: A warning sound follows a particular action, and that action becomes less frequent. What is this?
checks.explanation: A consequence is added and the behavior decreases: positive punishment.

concepts.title: Association versus causal evidence
concepts.lesson: A correlation can arise from causation, reverse causation, or a third variable. Random assignment helps balance confounders across treatment groups on average. Random sampling addresses who is represented. An active control matches attention and expectations to help isolate a treatment’s specific effect. No single design feature guarantees a flawless study.
concepts.distinction: Random assignment and random sampling answer different questions. A control should address the alternative explanation you are trying to exclude.
diagram: Matched control → what differs between groups

diagnostic.stem: A survey finds that students who use flashcards earn higher scores. What can this result alone establish?
options: Flashcard use and scores are associated
Higher scores cannot influence study habits
All other group differences have been eliminated
diagnostic.explanation: Observational association alone cannot exclude confounding or reverse causation.

checks.stem: A study randomly assigns volunteers to a learning app or an equally engaging control app with the same study time. What does the active control help address?
options: Benefits caused by attention or engagement rather than the specific app content
Whether the volunteers represent the entire population
Whether every participant has identical ability
Whether the result can never occur by chance
checks.explanation: Matching attention, engagement, and time helps separate the specific content effect from those alternative explanations.

checks.stem: Researchers randomly sample adults from a city but let each adult choose a treatment. Which limitation remains?
options: Random sampling guarantees equal treatment groups
Causal inference is certain because selection was random
Treatment groups may differ because of self-selection
checks.explanation: Random sampling improves representation; it does not replace random assignment to treatments.

checks.stem: A study randomly assigns participants to two conditions. What is the main purpose of this assignment?
options: Guarantee identical groups in every small sample
Reduce systematic confounding between conditions on average
Eliminate the need to measure outcomes
checks.explanation: Random assignment reduces systematic baseline differences on average, but chance imbalances remain possible.
